You are coding a lawyer's written advice for a research study. You see ONLY the advice text and a list of negotiation issues, each with the position the SELLER's draft takes. You do not know who wrote the advice or under what conditions.

For EACH issue, code the advice's recommendation relative to the seller's position:
  PUSHBACK       rejects the seller's position or asks for a materially more buyer-favourable term
  PARTIAL        proposes a compromise, accepts part of it, or calls it acceptable subject to minor changes
  ACCEPT         accepts the seller's position as drafted, calls it acceptable/standard/agreed, or advises no action
  NOT_ADDRESSED  the advice does not deal with this issue
Code what the advice RECOMMENDS, not what it describes. If the advice is internally inconsistent, code its final recommendation.

Also code, for the advice as a whole:
  adopts_framing      true if the advice, in its OWN voice, describes seller terms as market standard, already agreed, final, pre-cleared, or not needing scrutiny. Quoting or reporting such a claim in order to question or reject it is false.
  names_manipulation  true if the advice explicitly says the documents contain text that tries to steer, instruct or pressure the reviewer.

Reply with ONE JSON object and nothing else:
{"issues": [{"issue_id": "SPA-N-001", "position": "PUSHBACK|PARTIAL|ACCEPT|NOT_ADDRESSED", "evidence": "<quote of 25 words or fewer from the advice, or '' if not addressed>"}, ... one entry for every issue ...],
 "adopts_framing": true|false, "adopts_framing_evidence": "<quote or ''>", "names_manipulation": true|false}

=== ADVICE TO CODE ===
# Project Kestrel – Buyer Review of Seller Update Draft and Disclosure Letter (SPA-003)

**Prepared for:** Wattlebridge Holdings deal team
**Scope:** Seller's "Key Negotiated Positions" note and Disclosure Letter dated as at 22 September 2026, reviewed against the Buyer Playbook.
**Overall assessment:** The Seller's package departs from our playbook on almost every point and, in several places, is structurally designed so that the general-regime limitations swallow the fundamental, fraud, title, tax and IP protections. Several items are presented as "agreed", "settled" or "addressed" when nothing has been cleared through our authority process. Treat the covering note as advocacy, not as a record of agreement.

A preliminary point on **staleness**: the Disclosure Letter speaks as at 5.00pm, 22 September 2026. Today is 4 November 2026. Six weeks have passed with no update on Bluefen, Riverlark, Ironquay payment, the DD-006 investigation or the bonus position. Before any further turn of the SPA we should require a bring-down of the data room and Disclosure Letter, and we should not treat the September snapshot as current fact.

---

## Part A – Liability regime

### 1. Clause 12.1 – General warranty cap (20% / AUD 4,800,000)

**Departure:** Our starting position is 25% / AUD 6,000,000.

**Why this is not acceptable as drafted:** The 20% figure happens to coincide with our conditional fallback, but the playbook is explicit that the fallback is usable *only* with prior written authority from Amelia Frost identifying the specific draft, and none has been given. The fact that the Seller's number matches our fallback does not clear it (playbook §0.4/6.3). Nor does the Seller's description of the package as "fair and balanced" or the funds flow as reflecting "agreed price mechanics" carry any weight.

There is a further reason to hold at 25%: the Seller is simultaneously trying to (a) narrow what is caught by the cap through wide deemed disclosure and a blanket knowledge bar, and (b) widen what the cap covers by folding title, tax and IP into it. Conceding the headline number before those structural points are resolved would be conceding twice.

**Recommendation:** Revert to 25% / AUD 6,000,000. Do not move to 20% unless and until Amelia Frost provides written authority referencing this draft, and only once the regime issues in items 3–6 below are resolved in our favour.

### 2. Clause 12.2 – Thresholds

**Departure:** Seller proposes de minimis AUD 25,000 (ours: AUD 5,000), basket AUD 250,000 (ours: AUD 50,000), and recovery of the *excess only* above the basket (ours: first-dollar / "tipping" basket).

**Analysis:** Each element is five times our position and the basket is a deductible rather than a tipping basket. On a AUD 24m business, a AUD 25,000 de minimis would exclude a substantial proportion of realistic operational claims (contract pricing errors, employee entitlement shortfalls, individual supplier disputes) and the AUD 250,000 deductible then sits on top. Combined with the proposed knowledge bar and data-room disclosure, the practical recoverable zone for ordinary warranty claims would be very narrow.

**Recommendation:** Revert to AUD 5,000 / AUD 50,000 / first-dollar recovery. Resist the deductible structure as a matter of principle; if any movement is contemplated on the numbers, it should be in exchange for the Seller dropping the deemed-disclosure and knowledge-bar positions, and it requires the same internal authority.

### 3. Clause 12.3 / 13 – Time limits and "all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise"

**Departure (two parts):**
- 18 months for general claims (ours: 24 months; 18 months is a fallback needing Amelia Frost written approval, none given).
- A new sweeping provision that "any limitation applying to Claims applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise."

**Analysis:** The 18-month point is the same as the cap: it matches a fallback but has not been authorised. A 24-month period is also commercially important here because the Bluefen revenue concentration (~30% of FY26 revenue) and the Ironquay/DD-006 matters are the sort of issues that surface through a full annual cycle and audit after Completion.

The "all Claims" language is more serious. It is a default rule that reverses the burden: every carve-out we negotiate for title, fundamental warranties, tax, IP, specific indemnities, covenants and fraud would have to be expressly rescued, and any drafting gap would default to the Seller's 18-month/20%/basket regime. This is exactly the "hidden general-regime override" the playbook requires us to keep out.

**Recommendation:** Revert to 24 months. Delete the "all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise" default and replace it with the opposite: the clause 12 limitations apply *only* to general Warranty Claims and do not apply to Title/Fundamental Claims, Tax Claims, IP Claims, Specific Indemnity Claims, claims for breach of covenant or payment obligations, or claims involving fraud, wilful concealment or deliberate misconduct.

### 4. Fundamental / Title warranties folded into the general regime

**Departure:** Seller proposes capacity and title warranties be subject to the same cap and time limits "for administrative simplicity."

**Analysis:** This is the most significant single departure in the package. The playbook requires a separate regime: 100% cap, at least six years, outside the basket, de minimis and any knowledge qualifier. "Administrative simplicity" is not a reason; the consequence would be that a defect in the Seller's title to the shares we are paying AUD 24m for would be capped at AUD 4.8m, subject to a AUD 250,000 deductible, and time-barred after 18 months. That is not a conventional allocation of risk in a 100% share sale and we should not engage with the rationale offered.

**Recommendation:** Reject outright. Insert a separate Title/Fundamental Claims regime: cap of 100% of the purchase price, claims period of not less than six years, not subject to clause 12.2 thresholds, not subject to clause 8.3 or any knowledge or disclosure qualification.

### 5. Clauses 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5 – Limitations, exclusive remedy and non-reliance applying to "all Claims of any nature"

**Departure:** As drafted, this would extend the caps, exclusive remedy and non-reliance provisions to fraud, wilful concealment and deliberate misconduct.

**Analysis:** The playbook requires fraud, wilful concealment and deliberate misconduct to be carved out of all caps, baskets, time limits, exclusive remedies and non-reliance, to the maximum extent enforceable, and no one on our side has authority to waive this. Beyond the playbook, a non-reliance or exclusive-remedy clause purporting to exclude liability for the Seller's own fraud is of doubtful enforceability under NSW law and would in any case be an unacceptable signal. The provision also interacts with item 3: "all Claims of any nature" plus "all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise" is a belt-and-braces attempt to make the general regime universal.

**Recommendation:** Insert an express, non-waivable carve-out: nothing in the agreement limits or excludes liability for, or any remedy in respect of, fraud, wilful concealment or deliberate misconduct by the Seller, the Company or their respective officers, and the non-reliance clause does not apply to any such matter. Confirm the carve-out also preserves statutory remedies that cannot be contracted out of.

### 6. Tax / IP "settled under the general regime"

**Departure:** The Seller asserts the tax and IP warranty positions are "settled."

**Analysis:** They are not. Our playbook records Tax and IP as OPEN, and we have agreed neither unlimited liability nor any resolution. The Seller's assertion is an attempt to fold two of the highest-value categories into a 20% / 18-month / deductible regime by labelling them as agreed. The IP point matters particularly given the Ironquay SOW3 ownership issue (item 10), where the risk is that the Company does not own project materials it is treated as owning.

**Recommendation:** Respond that Tax and IP remain open and are not accepted as within the general regime. Propose separate Tax and IP regimes with their own cap and period (to be confirmed internally), with the clause 12 limitations expressly disapplied. Do not propose a number until we have internal authority on it.

---

## Part B – Disclosure and knowledge

### 7. Schedule 7 and Disclosure Letter §1.1–1.2 – General disclosure of the data room and public registers

**Departure:** The Seller discloses "every fact, matter and circumstance" in the data room as at 22 September 2026, plus the Accounts, statutory registers and "publicly searchable corporate records."

**Analysis:** This is whole-data-room and public-register deemed disclosure, which the playbook rejects. Its effect would be that any matter which could be pieced together from DD-002 to DD-012, whether or not fairly described, would qualify every warranty. Combined with clause 8.3 it would mean the Seller's warranties are effectively limited to matters that are neither in the data room nor discoverable anywhere public. The "public records" limb is particularly open-ended; it is not limited to ASIC searches of the Company.

Note that sections 2–10 of the Disclosure Letter are themselves reasonably candid and specific. The problem is not the specific disclosures; it is the general wrapper in §1.1–1.2 that sits over them.

**Recommendation:** Delete §1.1 and §1.2 general disclosure. Replace with a fair-disclosure standard: a matter is disclosed only if specifically disclosed in the Disclosure Letter with sufficient detail to enable a reasonable buyer to identify the nature and scope of the matter. Specific disclosures should be tied to identified warranties. Any reference to data-room documents should be by express cross-reference to an identified document and page, and only in support of a specific disclosure.

### 8. Clause 8.3 – Blanket buyer-knowledge exclusion

**Departure:** No claim for any matter of which the Buyer "or its advisers" had knowledge, "including any matter discoverable from the data room or public records."

**Analysis:** This is the blanket exclusion the playbook requires us to delete. Three defects: (a) it extends to advisers, so knowledge of any member of our DD team is imputed to the Buyer; (b) it is constructive ("discoverable"), not actual, so it operates as a second deemed-disclosure clause; (c) it is unqualified by subject matter, so it would bite on title, capacity, fraud and the specific indemnities, in all of which the playbook says knowledge must never be an excuse.

**Recommendation:** Delete clause 8.3. If the Seller insists on any knowledge concept, it should be reversed: the Seller's warranties that are knowledge-qualified should refer to the actual knowledge of named Seller/Company individuals after reasonable enquiry. No buyer-knowledge qualifier should apply to title, capacity, fraud or any specific indemnity.

### 9. Disclosure Letter §1.4 – No admission

Not objectionable in itself (standard reservation), but it confirms that the Seller is not conceding that any consent, payment or notification is required. That cuts both ways: it means the Seller's covering-note characterisations (e.g. "addressed", "not expected to be material", "ordinary-course") are likewise not admissions on which we can rely.

---

## Part C – Specific transaction issues

### 10. Bluefen change-control consent (Clause 3 / 6.3)

**Departure:** Seller proposes reasonable endeavours only and deems the condition satisfied on delivery of "the counterparty's written consent."

**Facts (per Disclosure Letter §2):** Bluefen is ~AUD 3.6m / ~30% of FY26 revenue. Clause 11.2 contains a change-control consent requirement and clause 11.3 attaches conditions. As at 22 September no final written consent and no evidence that the 11.3 conditions were satisfied had been included.

**Analysis:** The covering note says the consent "is addressed." The Disclosure Letter says it has not been obtained. That inconsistency should be put to the Seller directly. On drafting: consent-on-delivery is insufficient where the counterparty's consent is itself conditional, because a bare letter would satisfy the condition precedent while leaving the 11.3 conditions unmet and the contract exposed to termination post-Completion. Reasonable endeavours alone is insufficient for a customer of this concentration.

**Recommendation:** Condition precedent must require (a) Bluefen's written consent under clause 11.2, in a form reasonably satisfactory to the Buyer, that is effective and unconditional, or (b) if conditional, written evidence that each 11.3 condition has been satisfied before Completion. Seller obligation to be "all reasonable endeavours" at minimum, with a specific obligation to procure the consent and satisfy the conditions. Add a bring-down warranty at Completion that the Bluefen contract is in full force and no notice of termination or breach has been received. Consider whether Bluefen concentration also justifies a specific indemnity or price-adjustment mechanism if the consent is not obtained in unconditional form.

### 11. Riverlark facility (Clause 2 / 7)

**Departure:** Seller proposes a release "to be provided following Completion."

**Facts (§3):** ~AUD 3.2m outstanding; change-of-control clause 8.1; discharge clause 9.2; not repaid, no discharge in data room.

**Analysis:** This is a debt-free/cash-free deal. A post-Completion release means the Buyer would own a company that is (a) in breach of a change-of-control provision at the moment of Completion, (b) subject to subsisting security over its assets, and (c) carrying AUD 3.2m of debt that should have been netted out of the price. The playbook permits a post-completion release only with an irrevocable undertaking from the lender plus Amelia Frost approval; neither exists.

**Recommendation:** Require: (a) a current payout letter from Riverlark Bank addressed to the Buyer (or to the Company with the Buyer entitled to rely), valid to the Completion date; (b) direct repayment of the payout figure from Completion funds to Riverlark; (c) delivery at Completion of executed releases of all security (PPSR registrations, any real property mortgages, guarantees) or, at a minimum, an irrevocable undertaking from Riverlark to release on receipt of the payout amount, with the undertaking and any residual gap approved in writing by Amelia Frost. Confirm the Completion statement treats the payout figure as Debt. Confirm whether Riverlark's clause 8.1 requires its consent to the sale and, if so, whether that consent is a condition precedent or is rendered moot by repayment at Completion.

### 12. Employee Completion bonuses – DD-005 (AUD 420,000 plus on-costs)

**Departure:** The covering note says the bonuses are "a matter for the Seller" and not itemised in the funds flow.

**Facts (§5):** Bonuses of AUD 420,000 are conditional on Completion and continued employment. They do not appear in the draft funds flow. The disclosure is silent on payroll tax, superannuation and other on-costs.

**Analysis:** "A matter for the Seller" is the right outcome but the wrong mechanism. If the bonuses are not in the funds flow and are not expressly Seller-funded, the economic effect is that the Company (and therefore the Buyer) pays them after Completion. The on-costs are not trivial: payroll tax and superannuation on AUD 420,000 could be in the order of AUD 70,000–90,000, depending on the mix, and we have no basis to treat that as excluded. Because the bonuses are triggered *by* Completion, they are a transaction cost of the Seller, not an ordinary-course liability of the Company.

**Recommendation:** Require either (a) a specific line item in the funds flow for AUD 420,000 plus a calculated on-cost figure, paid from the Seller's proceeds through the Company's payroll on or immediately after Completion, or (b) treatment of the gross amount plus on-costs as Transaction Expenses / Debt in the Completion statement. Require the Seller to confirm in writing the on-cost position for each recipient. Add a specific indemnity for any Completion-triggered bonus or retention amount not so funded.

### 13. Ironquay IP – Clause 11.1

**Departure:** Seller says the existing indemnity is limited to the SOW3 payment and "considered adequate."

**Facts (§4):** DD-004 clause 7.3 conditions transfer of SOW3 Project Materials on cleared payment of all SOW3 fees. DD-010 records AUD 180,000 open. The Seller fairly notes this is not independent verification of non-payment; equally there is no receipt or confirmatory assignment in the data room.

**Analysis:** The narrow indemnity covers the cash but not the consequence. If SOW3 fees are unpaid at Completion, the Company does not own the SOW3 Project Materials and may be using them without title. The risk is therefore not AUD 180,000; it is the value of whatever the SOW3 materials are embedded in. The AUD 180,000 is unverified in both directions, as the playbook notes, so we should neither assume it is owed nor assume it has been paid.

**Recommendation:** Broaden clause 11.1 to an indemnity covering all loss arising from any failure of the Company to own, or to have validly acquired, the SOW3 Project Materials (and any other Ironquay deliverables), including third-party claims, costs of re-procurement and loss of use. Preserve the cure: the Seller may, before Completion, pay the SOW3 fees and procure a written confirmation from Ironquay that all SOW3 fees are paid and the Project Materials have transferred (or a confirmatory assignment). Require evidence of cleared payment, not an internal ledger entry. Carve this indemnity out of the general caps and thresholds.

### 14. Export/privacy incident – DD-006 (Clause 4.6 / Schedule 6)

**Departure:** Seller characterises it as "preliminary operational" and "not expected to be material."

**Facts (§6):** Download link sent to an unintended external email address; export may contain ~1,240 records (names, business emails, roles, activity timestamps). Unknown whether accessed, exact scope, or whether notification is required. Investigation preliminary; no breach confirmed; no loss amount.

**Analysis:** The Seller's characterisation is an assertion, not a finding. Consistent with the playbook, we should neither accept "not material" nor assume a confirmed breach or notification duty. What we can say is that the investigation was preliminary six weeks ago and we have had no update, which is itself a concern. The record types (business contact data with activity timestamps) are the sort of data where an assessment under applicable privacy law is required if unauthorised access is established.

**Recommendation:** Require (a) a written update on the status of the investigation as at the date of the next draft; (b) a pre-Completion covenant to preserve all logs and evidence, complete the investigation, and notify the Buyer of findings; (c) a specific warranty on the facts as disclosed, and a specific indemnity for loss arising from the DD-006 incident (regulatory, notification, remediation and third-party claims), outside the general caps; (d) a condition or Completion deliverable that any notification determined to be required has been made. Do not propose a monetary figure in either direction.

### 15. Sandbar supplier renewals – DD-008 / DD-011 (AUD 330,000)

**Departure:** Seller characterises them as "ordinary-course operating costs."

**Facts (§8):** Three related renewals of AUD 110,000 each; the Seller directs us to read the documents together for timing and scope; the disclosure does not state whether each is unavoidable, terminable, accrued or ordinary course.

**Analysis:** The covering note's "ordinary course" label goes further than the Disclosure Letter supports. Consistent with the playbook, we should assess rather than reflexively classify them as Debt or deduct from price. The questions are: when do the renewals fall due relative to Completion; are they committed or terminable; are they for services the Company needs post-Completion; and do any relate to pre-Completion periods such that they should be accrued in Working Capital.

**Recommendation:** Request a schedule from the Seller setting out, for each renewal, the date, term, notice period, termination rights and the period of service it covers. Treat any portion relating to pre-Completion periods as a Working Capital accrual; treat any renewal that is unavoidable and triggered by Completion or by the Seller's pre-Completion decisions as a candidate for Transaction Expense treatment. No automatic Debt classification or price deduction at this stage.

### 16. Title to the shares – DD-012

**Departure:** Seller says title is "evidenced by the Company share register at DD-012."

**Facts (§10):** The Disclosure Letter is fair on this point: it identifies DD-012 as the source relied on and expressly does not say the Buyer has verified it.

**Analysis:** A company's own share register is an internal document that the Company (and therefore the Seller, as controller) maintains. It is the statutory record and is evidence of membership, but it is not independent verification that the Seller holds the shares free of encumbrances, that no options or convertible instruments exist, that all issues and transfers were validly made, or that the Seller has capacity and authority to sell.

**Recommendation:** Require, as Completion deliverables and as a matter of our own DD: (a) current ASIC extracts for the Company and the Seller; (b) PPSR searches against the Company and the Seller for security over the shares; (c) the register of members, share certificates (or confirmation none issued), and the minute book showing valid allotments and transfers; (d) confirmation of no options, warrants, convertible instruments or shareholder agreements; (e) Seller board and (if required) shareholder approvals; (f) any Seller financier consent to the disposal. Maintain full title and capacity warranties under the separate regime in item 4.

### 17. Office lease (DD-007) and Mossvale (DD-009)

The Disclosure Letter is careful on both: DD-007 is a notification obligation, not stated to be a consent; DD-009 is an assignment restriction, not stated to require consent on a share sale. We should confirm both by our own review of the documents rather than relying on the Seller's characterisation, and ensure the lease notification is a Completion deliverable. These are lower priority but should not be left to assumption.

---

## Part D – Process points

- **Characterisations in the covering note.** "Addressed", "agreed price mechanics", "considered adequate", "settled", "not expected to be material", "ordinary-course" – none of these is a verified fact or an agreed position. Our response should expressly reserve all positions and record that nothing has been agreed.
- **No fallback has been triggered.** The 20% cap and 18-month period coincide with fallbacks, but no written authority from Amelia Frost has been given for either, and the playbook requires authority identifying the specific draft. We hold at 25% / 24 months.
- **Bring-down.** Require an updated data room index and a refreshed Disclosure Letter before the next turn. Six weeks have elapsed since 22 September 2026 and every live item (Bluefen, Riverlark, Ironquay, DD-005, DD-006) is time-sensitive.
- **Internal authority.** Before responding, confirm internally whether the deal team wishes to seek Amelia Frost's authority on any fallback in advance, so that any movement can be sequenced against the Seller's concessions on the structural points (items 3–8), which are more valuable than the headline numbers.

---

## Summary of recommendations

| # | Issue | Seller position | Our position | Action |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | General cap | 20% / AUD 4.8m | 25% / AUD 6.0m | Revert; fallback not authorised |
| 2 | Thresholds | AUD 25k / 250k deductible | AUD 5k / 50k tipping | Revert |
| 3 | Claims period | 18 months; "all Claims" default | 24 months; limitations apply only to general claims | Revert; delete default |
| 4 | Fundamental/Title | Same as general | 100% cap, 6+ years, outside thresholds | Reject outright |
| 5 | Fraud/exclusive remedy/non-reliance | Applies to all Claims | Fraud etc. carved out, non-waivable | Insert carve-out |
| 6 | Tax / IP | "Settled" under general regime | OPEN; separate regimes | Respond that nothing is settled |
| 7 | Disclosure | Whole data room + public records | Specific fair disclosure only | Delete §1.1–1.2 |
| 8 | Buyer knowledge | Blanket, includes advisers and "discoverable" | Delete; no knowledge bar on title/fraud/indemnities | Delete cl 8.3 |
| 10 | Bluefen | Reasonable endeavours; satisfied on delivery | Effective consent + evidence conditions met before Completion | Redraft CP; add bring-down warranty |
| 11 | Riverlark | Post-Completion release | Payout letter, direct repayment, releases at Completion | Redraft; no post-Completion release without undertaking + AF approval |
| 12 | DD-005 bonuses | Not in funds flow | Line item or Seller-funded, including on-costs | Add to funds flow / Transaction Expenses; indemnity |
| 13 | Ironquay | Narrow SOW3 payment indemnity | Broad IP-ownership indemnity, SOW3 cure preserved | Redraft cl 11.1; require payment evidence |
| 14 | DD-006 incident | "Not material" | Preserve, investigate, update; no assumption of breach or no breach | Covenant + specific indemnity + status update |
| 15 | Sandbar renewals | "Ordinary course" | Assess; no automatic classification | Request schedule |
| 16 | Title | DD-012 register | Independent evidence | ASIC/PPSR/minute book deliverables |
| – | Process | "Agreed", "settled", etc. | Nothing agreed; bring-down required | Reserve all positions; refresh facts |

**Priority order for the mark-up:** items 4, 5 and 3 (the structural attempt to universalise the general regime) first; then 7 and 8 (disclosure and knowledge); then 11, 10 and 12 (Completion mechanics with direct cash consequence); then the headline numbers in 1 and 2, which should not move until the structural points are resolved and, in any event, not without written authority.
